subject: EM
title: Agriculture & soils
sub: Soils, farming systems, impacts, sustainable farming
strategyIntro: Environmental Management has no Core or Extended split. The full exam is Paper 1 (theory: short questions, then longer questions using source material) and Paper 2 (management in context, based on one country). Most marks come from reading sources and building arguments.

strategy.title: Quote the data
points: Most marks come from graphs, tables and maps.
Use figures with units: “fell from 62% to 41%” scores; “it fell” doesn’t.
Describe the overall trend first, then give the highest, lowest or any exception.

strategy.title: The 6-mark argument
points: Usually one per paper: discuss a statement for and against.
Structure: two points for, two against, then a conclusion.
Each point needs a reason: say why it matters, not just what it is.

strategy.title: Use named examples
points: Name a real crop, farming method or country where you can (e.g. terracing in Nepal, drip irrigation in Israel).
On Paper 2, link every answer back to the country in the source. General answers score lower.

strategy.title: Fieldwork comes up every year
points: Know sampling, quadrats, questionnaires and how to make them reliable.
Evaluate a method: one strength, one weakness, one improvement.

commandWords: Give a short fact. No explanation needed.
Say what happens or what you see. With data, quote figures and units.
Say why or how. Use “because” and link cause to effect.
Apply what you know to a new situation. Any sensible reason scores.
Give similarities or differences for both things in the same sentence.
Show working and give the unit.
Weigh up both sides and finish with a judgement.
quizIntro: These are not exam-format questions (EM has no multiple choice). Use them to check the facts are secure before you try the longer questions.
flashIntro: Say each definition out loud before you tap, then check you used the exact keywords.

flashcards.back: A mixture of mineral particles, organic matter (humus), water, air and living organisms.
Dark, decomposed organic matter in soil. It holds water and nutrients and improves soil structure.
Sand is the largest, then silt; clay particles are the smallest.
Large particles and air spaces: drains quickly, well aerated, easy to dig, but dries out and loses nutrients by leaching.
Tiny particles: holds water and nutrients well, but can become waterlogged, is poorly aerated and heavy to dig.
A soil with a balanced mix of sand, silt and clay plus humus. Holds water and nutrients but still drains: best for most crops.
Nutrients dissolve in water and are washed down through the soil, out of reach of plant roots.
The three main nutrients in fertiliser: nitrogen (leaf growth, proteins), phosphorus (roots), potassium (flowers, fruit, disease resistance).
Most crops grow best at pH 6–7. Adding lime (calcium carbonate) raises the pH of an acidic soil.
Earthworms mix and aerate soil and drag in leaves; bacteria and fungi decompose dead matter, releasing nutrients.
Growing crops, e.g. wheat, rice, maize.
Rearing animals, e.g. cattle, sheep, goats. Mixed farming does both.
Producing food mainly to feed the farmer’s own family, with little or nothing left to sell.
Producing crops or animals to sell for profit, often on a large scale.
High inputs of labour or money (machinery, fertiliser, feed) per unit area to get high yields from a small area.
Low inputs per unit area, usually over large areas, giving lower yields per hectare, e.g. sheep on hill land.
Manufactured chemicals containing nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium (NPK), added to soil to increase crop growth.
Chemical that kills organisms that harm crops: insecticides (insects), herbicides (weeds), fungicides (fungi).
Choosing parents with useful features (e.g. high yield, disease resistance) to breed from, over many generations. Gave the high-yielding varieties of the Green Revolution.
A crop whose genes have been changed by inserting a gene from another organism, e.g. to resist pests or tolerate drought.
Removal of topsoil by wind or water faster than new soil can form.
Keeping too many animals on land, so vegetation is eaten faster than it regrows and soil is left bare.
Land in dry areas becoming desert-like, caused by overgrazing, overcultivation, deforestation and drought.
Build-up of salts in the soil when irrigation water evaporates in hot, dry places, leaving the salts behind. Crops cannot grow.
Soil saturated with water, so roots lack oxygen. Can be caused by over-irrigation and poor drainage.
Nutrient enrichment of water (e.g. fertiliser runoff) causing algal blooms, then oxygen loss when the algae die and decompose.
Build-up of a persistent chemical (e.g. a pesticide) in an organism’s body over its lifetime.
Concentration of a persistent chemical increasing at each trophic level up a food chain, e.g. DDT in birds of prey.
Growing one crop over a large area. Problems: low biodiversity, pests spread easily, same nutrients used up each year.
Pests evolve so the pesticide no longer kills them: resistant individuals survive and breed (natural selection).
Cutting flat steps into a hillside. Slows runoff, so less soil is washed away, and creates flat land to farm.
Ploughing across a slope, along the contours. The ridges trap water and soil instead of channelling them downhill.
Growing two or more crops in the same field at the same time, so the ground stays covered and pests spread less.
Growing different crops in a field in successive years. Legumes add nitrogen; pest and disease cycles are broken.
Rows of trees or hedges that reduce wind speed across fields, cutting wind erosion.
Plants grown between main crops to keep the soil covered, bind it with roots and add organic matter.
Pipes deliver small amounts of water directly to plant roots. Little evaporation, so less water used and less salinisation.
Farming without artificial fertilisers or pesticides, using manure, compost, crop rotation and biological control.
Using a natural predator, parasite or disease to control a pest, e.g. ladybirds to eat aphids.
Moving animals between fields so grass can recover, preventing overgrazing.

quiz.q: Which soil particles are the smallest?
quiz.why: Clay particles are tiny, so the pores between them are tiny too. That is why clay holds water but drains slowly.

quiz.q: Why does sandy soil lose nutrients easily?
options: Large pore spaces let water drain through fast, leaching nutrients
Its particles are too small for roots to grow
quiz.why: Fast drainage carries dissolved nutrients down past the roots (leaching).

quiz.q: Which mineral ion do plants need to make chlorophyll?
quiz.why: Magnesium is at the centre of the chlorophyll molecule. Lack of it gives yellow leaves.

quiz.q: Loam is the best soil for most crops because it:
options: Holds water and nutrients but still drains well
quiz.why: The mix of particle sizes gives both water retention and drainage; humus adds nutrients.

quiz.q: A farmer adds lime to a field in order to:
options: Raise the pH of acidic soil
quiz.why: Lime (calcium carbonate) neutralises acidity, bringing the pH up towards 6–7.

quiz.q: A family grows maize and beans to feed themselves and sells almost nothing. This is:
quiz.why: Subsistence = growing food mainly for your own family.

quiz.q: Which is an example of intensive farming?
options: Cattle ranching on huge unfenced grassland
quiz.why: Glasshouses use large inputs of money and energy on a small area to get very high yields.

quiz.q: Hydroponics means:
options: Growing plants in a nutrient solution without soil
quiz.why: Roots sit in water with dissolved mineral nutrients; often used in glasshouses with controlled light and temperature.

quiz.q: Which input increases yield mainly by reducing competition for light, water and nutrients?
quiz.why: Herbicides kill weeds, which compete with the crop for light, water and nutrients.

quiz.q: One advantage of a pest-resistant GM crop is that:
options: Less insecticide needs to be sprayed
It increases biodiversity on the farm
quiz.why: The crop makes its own toxin to insect pests, so the farmer can spray less. Concerns include cost of seed and genes spreading to wild plants.

quiz.q: In eutrophication, what directly causes fish to die?
options: Algae release poison into the water
Bacteria decomposing dead algae and plants use up the dissolved oxygen
quiz.why: Order: nutrients → algal bloom → light blocked, plants die → decomposers multiply and respire → oxygen falls → fish suffocate.

quiz.q: Salinisation is most likely where:
options: Fields are irrigated in a hot, dry climate
Fields are ploughed along the contours
quiz.why: High evaporation draws water up and leaves the dissolved salts in the topsoil.

quiz.q: Which farming practice increases the risk of soil erosion?
options: Ploughing up and down a slope
quiz.why: Furrows running downhill channel rainwater, which carries soil away.

quiz.q: Why were birds of prey worst affected by DDT?
options: They ate the crops that were sprayed
They drank more water than other animals
They are top predators, so DDT was most concentrated in them
quiz.why: Biomagnification: DDT is not broken down, so it concentrates at each level. It made eggshells thin, so few chicks hatched.

quiz.q: Overgrazing leads to soil erosion because:
options: Animals compact the soil so it holds more water
Animal dung adds too many nutrients
Vegetation is removed, leaving bare soil exposed to wind and rain
quiz.why: Without plant cover and roots, nothing holds the soil or shields it from rain splash and wind.

quiz.q: Terraces reduce soil erosion mainly because they:
options: Slow down water flowing down the slope
Stop all rain reaching the soil
quiz.why: Flat steps let water soak in rather than rushing downhill carrying soil.

quiz.q: Why are legumes (beans, peas, clover) included in a crop rotation?
options: Bacteria in their root nodules fix nitrogen, adding nitrates to the soil
They attract pests away from other crops
quiz.why: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria turn nitrogen gas into compounds plants can use, so less fertiliser is needed.

quiz.q: Drip irrigation reduces salinisation because:
options: It adds lime to the soil
Less water is used and less evaporates from the surface
quiz.why: Less evaporation means fewer salts are left behind in the topsoil.

quiz.q: A disadvantage of biological control is that:
options: Pests quickly become resistant to it
It is more toxic than pesticides
The control species may attack other, non-target species
quiz.why: Example: cane toads brought to Australia to eat beetles became a pest themselves.

quiz.q: Which method most directly reduces wind erosion?
quiz.why: Trees and hedges lower wind speed at ground level, so less soil is blown away.

examIntro: Paper 1 style. Write your answer first, then open the mark scheme. The data questions give a small table in the question: quote the figures in your answer.

exam.q: State two components of soil, other than mineral particles.
points: Organic matter / humus
Water
Air
Living organisms, e.g. earthworms, bacteria, fungi

exam.q: Compare the properties of sandy soil and clay soil.
points: Sandy soil has larger particles than clay
Sandy soil drains faster; clay holds more water / can waterlog
Clay holds more nutrients; sandy soil loses them by leaching
Sandy soil is better aerated than clay
Sandy soil is easier to dig / plough and warms up faster in spring
exam.note: Any 4. “Compare” means each point must mention both soils.

exam.q: A student poured 100 cm³ of water onto each of two 200 g soil samples in funnels. After 10 minutes, 74 cm³ had drained through soil A and 21 cm³ through soil B. (a) Calculate the percentage of the water retained by soil B. (b) Suggest which soil contains more clay, and explain why. (c) Suggest one way to make the test fair.
points: (a) 100 − 21 = 79 cm³ retained
(b) Soil B
(b) Clay has very small particles / small pore spaces, so water passes through slowly and is held
(c) Same mass of soil / same volume of water / same time / same size funnel and filter paper / both soils equally dry at the start

exam.q: State two differences between intensive and extensive farming.
points: Intensive has high inputs per hectare; extensive has low inputs
Intensive gets high yields per hectare; extensive gets low yields per hectare
Intensive usually uses a small area; extensive a large area
Intensive uses more machinery, fertiliser or labour per hectare

exam.q: Explain how two different methods can increase crop yields.
points: Method 1 named, e.g. inorganic fertiliser
Explanation, e.g. supplies nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium the soil lacks, so plants grow faster
Method 2 named, e.g. irrigation
Explanation, e.g. supplies water in the dry season, so crops do not wilt and more than one crop a year can be grown
Other methods: pesticides (fewer crops eaten or diseased), high-yielding varieties / selective breeding, GM crops, glasshouses (control temperature, light, CO2), mechanisation
exam.note: 1 mark for each method and 1 for each explanation.

exam.q: Wheat yield in Country Y (tonnes per hectare): 1960 – 1.2; 1980 – 2.1; 2000 – 3.0; 2020 – 3.4. Fertiliser use (kg per hectare): 1960 – 20; 1980 – 85; 2000 – 140; 2020 – 150. (a) Describe the change in wheat yield. (b) Calculate the percentage increase in yield from 1960 to 2020. (c) Suggest why yield increased more slowly after 2000.
points: (a) Yield increased throughout / nearly tripled
(a) From 1.2 to 3.4 tonnes per hectare; rose 0.9 each 20 years to 2000 but only 0.4 from 2000 to 2020
(c) Fertiliser use hardly increased after 2000 (140 to 150 kg/ha)
(c) Adding more fertiliser gives smaller extra gains / another factor such as water became limiting / soil degraded / droughts or climate change

exam.q: State two causes of soil erosion on farmland.
points: Overgrazing
Removing hedgerows / trees
Ploughing up and down slopes
Leaving soil bare between crops
Deforestation to create fields
Overcultivation / monoculture weakening soil structure

exam.q: Describe how the use of fertiliser on farmland can lead to the death of fish in a nearby lake.
points: Rain washes fertiliser (nitrates/phosphates) into the lake by runoff or leaching
Algae grow rapidly / algal bloom
Algae block light so plants below die
Algae and plants die
Bacteria decompose the dead material
Bacteria use up oxygen in respiration, so fish suffocate

exam.q: Concentration of a pesticide (parts per million) in a lake food chain: water 0.00005; plankton 0.04; small fish 0.5; large fish 2.0; fish-eating bird 25. (a) Calculate how many times greater the concentration is in the bird than in the small fish. (b) Explain the pattern shown. (c) Suggest one effect on the bird population.
points: (b) Concentration increases at each trophic level / biomagnification
(b) The pesticide is persistent: not broken down or excreted, stored in fat
(b) Each consumer eats many organisms from the level below, so the pesticide builds up
(c) Thin eggshells / fewer chicks / birds die, so the population falls

exam.q: Name two methods that reduce soil erosion on steep slopes.
points: Terracing
Contour ploughing
Planting trees / afforestation
Stone lines (bunds) along the contours
Keeping soil covered: cover crops / intercropping

exam.q: Explain how crop rotation helps to maintain soil fertility and reduce pests.
points: Different crops take different nutrients, so one nutrient is not used up
Legumes in the rotation fix nitrogen / add nitrates
Less inorganic fertiliser needed
Pests and diseases specific to one crop die out when their host crop is moved
So less pesticide is needed
exam.note: Any 4; at least one point on fertility and one on pests.

exam.q: “Organic farming should replace intensive farming.” Discuss this statement.
points: For: no artificial pesticides, so less biomagnification and harm to wildlife
For: no inorganic fertiliser runoff, so less eutrophication
For: manure, crop rotation and hedgerows improve soil structure and biodiversity
Against: yields are usually lower, so more land is needed to feed the same number of people
Against: food costs more; more labour needed
Against: may not feed a growing world population; more forest might be cleared for farmland
Conclusion: a judgement, e.g. a mix, using sustainable methods within intensive farms, is more realistic
exam.note: Two points for, two against, plus a conclusion. Max 5 without a conclusion.
